summary: A 1970 note by M. Elie with comments on memory allocation control commands named CEASE, ALL, GVB, RET and RFNM. These are commands relating to managing buffer space between hosts.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 68 proposes changing RFNM so the receiving host confirms a message only after it has received it. The host could say to continue, cease sending or repeat the message, combining flow control and error recovery.

questions: how should flow control and error recovery work
what did rfc 68 propose for rfnm
how does ack cease control message flow
subtitle: A proposal to combine acknowledgments, flow control and error recovery.

tldr.problem: The existing buffer allocation scheme uses parallel mechanisms, and an RFNM can arrive before the host has fully received and checked a message.
tldr.mechanism: The author proposes host acknowledgments after full reception: ACK CONTINUE, ACK CEASE or NAK REPEAT, with the receiving NCP controlling whether more data may be sent.
tldr.outcome: The proposed point-to-point procedure would combine flow control with end-to-end error detection and retransmission by the sending host.

today: The unit metadata records RFC 68 as Unknown and lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The RFC presents a proposal for changing acknowledgment, flow control and error recovery behavior.

sections.title: Why Change the Existing RFNM
sections.content:
The author says the existing buffer allocation scheme requires two parallel mechanisms and may be more complicated than necessary. The receiving IMP sends RFNM after reconstructing a message and transmitting its first packet to the host, but before the host has necessarily accepted the full message.

As a result, the sender may transmit another message before the receiving host has completed the first one. The note also points out that the current design does not ensure that message text arrived without altered bits.
sections.plainLanguage: The existing RFNM can be sent before the receiving host has accepted the whole message. That may let more data arrive while the host is still handling the earlier message.

sections.title: Three Replies from the Receiving Host
sections.content:
The proposal has the receiving host acknowledge correct reception of a full message. It can send ACK (CONTINUE) when space is available for another message, or ACK (CEASE) when no more space is available.

If the NCP detects an error, it can send NAK (REPEAT) to request retransmission. The sending host, rather than the IMP, would repeat the message; a lack of reply would also initiate repetition.
sections.plainLanguage: After receiving a whole message, the host can say to continue or stop. If it finds an error, it can ask the sending host to repeat the message.

sections.title: Flow Control Without Advance Allocation
sections.content:
The author says ACK CONTINUE should be sent only when the receiving host has space for another message, while ACK CEASE signals that it does not. A later ACK CONTINUE or RESUME can restart transmission.

The user process does not take part in allocation; it sees the transmission speed of its data vary. The author argues that this procedure could replace the existing memory allocation mechanism and would not keep IMP memory occupied longer, because the sending host performs repetitions.
sections.plainLanguage: The receiving system controls the flow by allowing more data only when it has room. The user program does not manage the buffer allocation itself.

references.text: Deloche, G., "Implementation of the Host-Host Software Procedures in GORDO", Network Working Group RFC 11, August 1969.
